notes.meaning: Paul looked directly at the council and declared that he had lived with a clear conscience before God his whole life. He was not claiming to be sinless, but explaining that he had always acted sincerely according to what he believed was right. Even during his past zeal and now in serving Christ, his true motive had been to obey God.

Ananias the high priest ordered the men standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. He was enraged that an accused prisoner spoke with such confidence and claimed complete innocence. Striking an untried prisoner was an unlawful act of violence by a judge.

Paul rebuked Ananias sharply, calling him a whitewashed wall because he pretended to judge by the law while breaking it himself. A whitewashed wall looks clean on the outside but hides dirt underneath, making it a picture of a hypocrite. Paul declared that God would strike him down, a warning that came true years later when Ananias was killed by assassins.
The bystanders challenged Paul for daring to insult God's high priest. In their eyes, the high priest held a sacred office appointed by God, so speaking roughly to him was treated as a grave offense.

Paul replied that he did not realize the man was the high priest, and he quoted Scripture forbidding evil words against a ruler. Commentators often explain that Paul had been away from Jerusalem for years, the office changed frequently, or he spoke without stopping to think. By citing God's law, Paul showed that he still honored the biblical command to respect authority.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom taught that Paul truly did not recognize the high priest due to his long absence from Jerusalem.

notes.meaning: Paul noticed that the council was divided between Pharisees and Sadducees, so he called out that he was a Pharisee on trial for his hope in the resurrection of the dead. Resurrection means the promise that God will raise the dead to life again. This was a central Christian truth that fulfilled the best of Pharisee teaching, and stating it shifted the council's focus.

As soon as Paul mentioned the resurrection, a sharp dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, splitting the whole assembly. Instead of working together to condemn Paul, the two factions turned against each other over their own deep doctrinal differences.

Luke explains the background of the conflict: the Sadducees denied that the dead will rise, and they rejected the existence of angels and spirits. In contrast, the Pharisees believed in all of these spiritual realities.

A loud uproar arose as some scribes from the Pharisees stood up to defend Paul. They declared that they found nothing wrong with him and suggested that a spirit or an angel might really have spoken to him.

The argument grew so violent that the Roman commander feared the men would tear Paul to pieces. He ordered his soldiers to go down, pull Paul away by force, and bring him safely back into the fortress.

The following night, the Lord Jesus appeared beside Paul in his cell and told him to take courage. Jesus assured him that just as he had faithfully testified in Jerusalem, he would also bear witness in Rome. This promise guaranteed that Paul would survive his present dangers.
When morning came, a group of hostile Jews formed a conspiracy against Paul. They bound themselves under a curse, swearing that they would neither eat nor drink until they had murdered him.
More than forty men joined in this deadly plot. Their large number and solemn oath showed how intense their hatred was and how serious the threat had become.
The plotters went to the chief priests and elders and confessed their solemn oath to kill Paul. They felt confident that these religious leaders hated Paul enough to support an assassination.

They asked the council leaders to send a request to the Roman commander, pretending they wanted to investigate Paul's case more carefully. The conspirators planned to ambush and kill Paul along the road before he ever reached the council chamber.
Paul's nephew learned about the ambush and went inside the Roman barracks to warn Paul. God used this young family member to uncover the secret plot and protect the apostle's life.

Paul called a centurion and asked him to take the young man to the commander because he had important news. Even though Christ had promised Paul that he would reach Rome, Paul still used sensible and ordinary means to protect his safety.
The centurion led the young man to the commander and explained that Paul the prisoner had requested the meeting. The Roman officers treated Paul with respect and acted promptly on his word.
The commander took the young man by the hand and led him aside to speak in private. This kind gesture put the youth at ease and showed the commander's willingness to listen.

The young man explained that the Jewish leaders had agreed to ask the commander to bring Paul to the council the next day under false pretenses. They claimed they wanted more information, but the hearing was only a trap.

He urged the commander not to give in to their request, revealing that more than forty men were waiting to ambush Paul. He explained that these men had sworn not to eat or drink until Paul was dead, and they were only waiting for the commander's consent.

The commander sent the young man away with strict instructions not to let anyone know he had reported the plot. Keeping the matter quiet prevented the plotters from learning that their ambush had been discovered.

The commander called two centurions and ordered a force of two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to prepare for Caesarea. They were told to leave at nine o'clock that evening under cover of darkness.

He also directed them to provide riding animals for Paul so he could travel safely to Governor Felix. Felix was the Roman governor of Judea who lived in Caesarea, the administrative center of the province.
The commander wrote an official letter to send along with Paul to the governor. Roman legal procedure required an escorting officer to provide a written summary of the prisoner's case.

The letter opened with the formal greeting of Claudius Lysias to His Excellency, Governor Felix. Claudius Lysias used his full name, which paired his Greek family name with the Roman name he received upon gaining citizenship.

Lysias wrote that the Jews had seized Paul and were about to kill him when he arrived with his troops to rescue him. He presented his actions in the best possible light, claiming he stepped in because he knew Paul was a Roman citizen, though he had actually learned that detail later.

Lysias explained that he brought Paul before the Jewish high council because he wanted to discover the specific charges against him. As the commanding officer, he needed to know whether Paul had broken any civil laws.

He reported that the accusations dealt only with questions about Jewish religious law, and that Paul had done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment under Roman law. This official finding showed that the Roman government found no legal guilt in Paul.

Lysias concluded by explaining that he sent Paul immediately to Felix after learning of a plot against the man's life. He also noted that he had ordered Paul's accusers to bring their complaints before the governor in Caesarea.

The soldiers carried out their orders and escorted Paul by night as far as Antipatris. This town lay roughly halfway between Jerusalem and Caesarea, far enough to place Paul beyond the danger of the ambush.

The next day, the foot soldiers returned to their barracks in Jerusalem, leaving the horsemen to ride on with Paul. With the initial danger behind them, the cavalry alone could escort Paul quickly and safely.

When the horsemen arrived in Caesarea, they delivered the commander's letter to Governor Felix and presented Paul to him. This transfer placed Paul securely under the protection of the highest Roman authority in the province.

Felix read the letter and asked Paul which province he came from, learning that he was from Cilicia. Roman officials routinely checked a prisoner's home territory to ensure they had proper jurisdiction to judge the matter.
Felix promised to hear Paul's case as soon as the accusers arrived from Jerusalem. In the meantime, he ordered Paul to be kept under guard in the government palace built by Herod the Great.
